# Tickets

The tickets (`tickets/<DATE>_<SLUG>.md`, with their `.plan.md` and `.lock.md` siblings) live on the branch `agent-data`, never on a code branch. A `tickets` link at the repository root, if present, is a possibly stale copy: never write there.

Read and change them with the `tickets` command, always run by its full name: `npx @openagt/skill-tickets@0.1`. Every change it makes is one commit on the `agent-data` branch, pushed straight to the remote when the project shares its records. Never pass `--local` or `--force`: they are a person's.

Every command prints one JSON document; a refusal is `{"ok":false,"reason":…}` with why on stderr, exit 1; a wrong command line prints the usage on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit 2. Every `<file>` below is a ticket's filename (`2042-01-01_some-ticket.md`) or the `tickets/…` path a queue entry links to; `put` also takes the ticket's `.plan.md` and `meta.json`.

## Read

```
npx @openagt/skill-tickets@0.1 list                 every open ticket, as one JSON array; a row: file, title, summary, date,
                                                    planned, and when set priority, topics, issue, pr (set: the ticket is in
                                                    review), waiting (what it waits on), effort, uncertainty, outdated (the
                         
… 3625 characters cut …
Priority: 0-10 [optional; 10: critical, act immediately; 0: only if capacity]
Topics: [list-of-topics] [optional]
Issue: [#42](https://example.com/org/repo/issues/42) [optional: the issue this ticket tracks]
PR: [#1790](https://example.com/org/repo/pull/1790) [optional: the pull request that closes it]
Waiting: what it waits on [optional: no agent is handed it until a person removes the line]

# Ticket title

## TLDR

...

## Why it matters

...

[optional: more, under any heading]
```

A ticket with a `PR:` line is in review: skip it when choosing work, and never queue it while the line stands; remove the line to have it worked again. A `Waiting:` line names what the ticket waits on outside the work: skip the ticket when choosing work, and never queue it, nor a plan for it, while the line stands; only a person removes the line, when the wait is over. `Priority:` is a bare whole number from 0 to 10 above the `# ` title; anything else queues at 5.

### A claim: `tickets/<DATE>_<SLUG>.lock.md`

One line, `CLAIMED: <holder>`. Written by `claim`, removed by `release` or `close`.

### A plan: `tickets/<DATE>_<SLUG>.plan.md`

```md
Effort: 0-10 [0: trivial, 10: takes months]
Uncertainty: 0-10 [0: no meaningful alternatives, 10: highly uncertain how to implement]
Outdated: yes [optional: the ticket changed in a way that makes the plan outdated; a plan written again leaves it out]

# [Plan] Ticket title

One sentence saying what this file holds.

## Problems [optional: what is uncertain to implement, and why]

## Solutions [optional: ways to solve each problem, shortcuts included]

## Considerations [optional: everything to weigh, edge cases included]

## Implementation [optional: the concrete plan]

[optional: more, under any heading]
```

`Effort:` and `Uncertainty:` are bare whole numbers above the title, else absent. The uncertainty counts *significant* alternatives, not variability like syntax, and decides whether a human is needed before the work: 0 means clearly not.

# `npx @openagt/start`: a second run, the link it prints, and Ctrl+C

## TLDR

Three fixes to the dashboard process `npx @openagt/start` runs:

1. **A second run fails** with `EADDRINUSE` while a dashboard already runs. Wanted: it adds its repo to the running dashboard and opens that project's page.
2. **It prints the id link** (`http://127.0.0.1:4200/gemstack-st99l0`) while the page shows `/gemstack`. Wanted: it prints the address the page shows.
3. **Ctrl+C hangs while a dashboard tab is open** (seen on 0.24.0): one `SIGINT` ran the close hooks, then the port stayed held for over two minutes with two tabs' connections open and the test browser still a child; a second `SIGINT` ended it. Wanted: one Ctrl+C stops it in a few seconds, open tabs or not.

## Why it matters

`npx @openagt/start` is the first thing a new user types; each of these makes it look broken.

/**

function guardOwnPageFetch(req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse): boolean {
  const site = req.headers['sec-fetch-site']
  if ((site === undefined || site === 'same-origin') && req.headers['sec-fetch-mode'] !== 'navigate') return true
  res.writeHead(403, { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }).end('forbidden')

function guardBrowserOrigin(req: IncomingMessage, res: ServerResponse): boolean {

text:
I've found the hang: pending calls never settle when the websocket closes, so `send` never rejects. On Ctrl+C, since Chrome shares the process group, it gets SIGINT too and starts dying, so the `Browser.close` call sent to the closing socket never gets a reply and never rejects, hanging forever — which explains the zombie child browser. There's also an issue where the second SIGINT falls through to default behavior since the listener was removed after firing once.

Separately, `bridgeBrowser.stop` awaits `launching`, so if a launch is mid-flight (downloading Chrome or waiting 30s for readiness), stop will block on that too. The fix should make `connectCdp` reject all pending calls on socket close/error, add a timeout around the close call itself, and introduce an overall shutdown deadline in `runDaemon` so a second signal or timeout forces exit. I'm also considering reordering shutdown so the dashboard server stops listening and frees the port early, before slower teardown hooks run. Now I want to check how a second run should attach a project to an already-running dashboard — looking at the modules RPC exports and whether the same-origin guard would reject a plain Node fetch that lacks an Origin header.
Found a likely Ctrl+C hang: a CDP call never settles when Chrome's socket closes. Now checking how a second run could reach the running dashboard.

I'm confirming that adding a project through this path still runs the project's own open hooks, and that the share flag stays false. I note the RPC handlers are context-based so this is mostly an implementation detail, and that a second run joining a different-port existing dashboard should just print and exit cleanly without the Ctrl+C hint, while a port collision with a non-OpenAgent process should still show the original error. Security-wise, there's no new exposure since RPC from a local Node process was already unauthenticated.

Now shifting to the Ctrl+C hang issue: the first cause is that closing the CDP connection never resolves because the socket closes without the pending send settling, since Chrome quits via the same signal — the fix is to reject pending requests when the websocket closes.

I should also abort an in-progress browser launch if it's still mid-download when stop is called, rather than waiting on it. I'm reconsidering the shutdown order too — closing the dashboard server first frees the port immediately, even though it disconnects open SSE tabs, which is an acceptable tradeoff. And I want an overall teardown deadline so a stuck step doesn't block forever: bound each step individually and add a final safety timer that force-exits the process. I'm also noting that bin.ts might keep the process alive afterward if some child handles aren't unref'd, so an explicit exit call after the CLI resolves may be needed.

I should think through test coverage too — a daemon test where the browser's close() never resolves, and a connectCdp test with a websocket server that closes mid-handshake. Since Chrome isn't spawned detached, it'll receive SIGINT naturally from the terminal, which simplifies things. I don't think there are relevant changes between versions worth digging into further.

# [Plan] `npx @openagt/start`: a second run, the link it prints, and Ctrl+C

How to fix the three faults of the dashboard process `npx @openagt/start` runs: the second run, the printed link and Ctrl+C.

## Problems

1. **A second run.** `runDaemon` (`packages/openagent/src/daemon.ts`) goes straight to `startDashboard`, and `listenDashboard` (`src/dashboard/server.ts`) rejects with `EADDRINUSE`. `runForegroundDaemonCmd` (`packages/start/src/cli.ts`) then prints `could not start the dashboard (listen EADDRINUSE …)` and exits 1. Nothing tells whether the port belongs to an OpenAgent dashboard, and the running dashboard has no RPC that does what `startedIn` does: find the listed project that holds a folder, or else add the folder.
2. **The printed link.** `onProject` in `cli.ts` builds `${url}/${encodeURIComponent(started.id)}`. The address a page shows comes from `projectAddresses` (`packages/openagent/dashboard/lib/route.ts`). That is the folder name, unless an earlier project in the registry has the same name or a module page uses it as its segment. Then the address is the id. The server knows the registry order. It does not know the page words: modules declare their `pages[].segment` in their browser JS, and only `useModules` reads them, in the browser.
3. **Ctrl+C hangs.** The hang is in the teardown that runs after the close hooks:
   - `connectCdp` (`src/browser-stream.ts`) leaves a pending `send` unsettled when the socket closes: no `close` or `error` listener rejects `pending`. Chrome is spawned without `detached`, so it is in the terminal's process group and gets the same SIGINT. It starts to quit, `cdp.call('Browser.close')` in `startBridgeBrowser`'s `close` never answers, and `await bridgeBrowser.stop()` blocks forever. `runtime.dispose()` and `dashboard.close()` never run, so the port stays held and the tabs' event streams stay open. text: The line count and effort/uncertainty labeling seem fine, so I'll finalize the report as is.

I wrote the plan, `tickets/2026-10-18_start-second-run-link-ctrl-c.plan.md` (Effort 4, Uncertainty 3), and published it on `agent-data`. I've also released my claim on the ticket and marked the queue entry done. No code changed, and I haven't run anything to confirm the causes below; they come from reading the code.

**What causes each problem:**
- **Ctrl+C hang:** the likeliest cause is a message to Chrome that never gets an answer. When the connection to Chrome closes, `connectCdp` (`packages/openagent/src/browser-stream.ts`) never gives up on a message still waiting for a reply. Chrome is started in the terminal's process group, so the same Ctrl+C reaches it and it starts quitting. The shutdown's `Browser.close` call then waits forever. Everything after it never runs, including the step that frees the port, so the port stays held and the tabs stay connected. The second Ctrl+C works only because Node's default handler kills the process.
- **Second run:** when the port is in use, the command just reports the `EADDRINUSE` error. There is no check for whether the port belongs to an OpenAgent dashboard, and no way to hand the running dashboard the new folder.
- **Printed link:** the command prints `/<id>`. The page instead shows the address worked out by `projectAddresses` in the browser, which is normally the folder name.

**What the plan proposes:**
- **Ctrl+C:**
  - Give up on waiting messages when the connection to Chrome closes.
  - Put a time limit on closing Chrome, and stop waiting for a Chrome launch that is still in progress.
  - Close the dashboard first, so the port is freed straight away.
  - Put an overall deadline on the shutdown, and make a second Ctrl+C exit straight away.
  - Have `bin.ts` exit explicitly when it's done.
- **Second run:** add a dashboard call (e.g. `sendStartedIn(folder)`) that finds or adds the project. The first run uses it in-process; a second run that finds the port in use sends it to the running dashboard, opens the project's page and exits 0. If another program holds the port, it shows a clearer error that suggests `--port`.
- **Printed link:** move `projectAddresses` into shared server code so the command can print the name address. It keeps opening the id link, which always works.

**One decision for you:** the server can't see the words that module pages use as their addresses. So if a folder has the same name as a page (e.g. a folder named `logs`), the printed link would be wrong. You can either accept that rare gap, or also have modules declare their pages in their `package.json` so the server can read them. That's a bigger change.
